blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Explain how a market system works through buyers, sellers, market equilibrium and market disequilibrium.

blocks.heading: Buyers, sellers and prices
blocks.text: A market system is a way of organising an economy in which buyers and sellers interact in markets, and the prices emerging from that interaction decide how scarce resources are allocated. No official tells the fisherman at Walvis Bay how many kob to land; the buyers' price does that. A Tokyo shopper choosing between two rice brands does the work a planner would otherwise do.

blocks.heading: Equilibrium and disequilibrium at Otavi
blocks.text: At the weekend maize market at Otavi, sellers bring 300 bags and buyers want 300 at N$95 a bag: planned buying equals planned selling, so N$95 is the market equilibrium price. At N$70, buyers plan 380 bags but sellers bring 240, so 140 planned purchases go unsatisfied: a shortage, which is market disequilibrium. At N$120, sellers bring 340 bags but buyers plan 260, leaving 80 unsold: a surplus.

blocks.heading: Minimum price or maximum price?
blocks.text: Learners often mix up a minimum price with a maximum price because both are official limits on a price. The legal direction decides which is which: a minimum price is a floor that sellers may not charge below; a maximum price is a ceiling that sellers may not charge above. Where the limit sits against equilibrium decides whether it bites. In the Otavi example, a floor of N$120, above the N$95 equilibrium, tends to leave a surplus; a ceiling of N$70, below it, tends to leave a shortage. A ceiling of N$120 would change nothing, because the market already clears at N$95.

blocks.heading: How well does the market system allocate?
blocks.text: A market system tends to direct resources towards the goods buyers want most: a good scarce relative to wants fetches a higher price, and the higher price rewards those who supply it. Yet the system may direct resources poorly. Where buyers cannot be charged for a good - clean air over Walvis Bay - no price rewards provision, so the market tends to under-provide it; and where a price ignores costs imposed on others, a factory that dirties water may expand even where the harm outweighs its output. Its success therefore depends on whether a price exists that carries the good's full cost.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: Opportunity cost (topic 1.3) explains the choice every market forces; the three allocation questions follow in section 2.2.2; markets that allocate badly are topic 2.10.
